title: How to Spot a Real Deal on Amazon: 7 Checks Before You Buy
h1: How to spot a real deal on Amazon
description: A real deal is a price below what the item usually sells for, not below an inflated list price. Seven quick checks for Amazon sales, from price history to seller names.
intro: A real deal is a price clearly below what the item has actually sold for recently. The crossed-out "list price" next to a sale tells you little on its own, so check price history, the seller and the exact model before you buy.

sections.h: 1. Is the price low compared with recent prices, not the list price?
sections.answer: Compare the sale price with the item's price over the last 90 days or more. If it sold at the "sale" price most of the year, it is not a real discount.
body: Amazon's own Alexa for Shopping assistant can show 30-, 90- and 365-day price history, according to Amazon, and third-party trackers chart prices too. Our price history guide shows how to read those charts.

sections.answer: Be skeptical of a list price you have never seen anyone charge. A large percentage off an inflated reference price is a common way to make an ordinary price look special.
body: The Federal Trade Commission's Guides Against Deceptive Pricing (16 CFR Part 233) say a former-price comparison should be based on a price the item was actually offered at, in good faith, for a reasonably substantial period. That is a good test to apply yourself.

sections.h: 3. Is it the exact model you researched?
sections.answer: Check the model number, not just the product name. Sale listings sometimes feature an older, smaller or bundle-stripped version of a popular item.
body: Tool kits are a common example: a bare tool without batteries looks far cheaper than the full kit. Confirm what is in the box on the product page.

sections.answer: Look at the "Ships from" and "Sold by" lines near the buy button. Items sold by Amazon or by the brand's own store are the lowest-risk choice.
body: Unknown sellers offering a famous brand far below everyone else deserve extra caution, especially for chargers, batteries and anything that touches food or skin.

sections.h: 5. Is a countdown timer pushing you?
sections.answer: A timer creates urgency but does not change whether the price is good. If you already know the item's usual price, you can decide in seconds; if you do not, let it go.
body: Big sale events repeat. Prime Day, Prime Big Deal Days, Black Friday and Cyber Monday all happen every year, and many prices return between them.

sections.h: 6. Does a coupon or Subscribe and Save change the math?
sections.answer: Check the final price at checkout. A clipped coupon or Subscribe and Save discount can make an unadvertised item cheaper than a featured deal.
body: Read the terms on subscriptions so you are not signed up for repeat deliveries you do not want.

sections.h: 7. Would you buy it at this price if it were not on sale?
sections.answer: If the honest answer is no, skip it. The cheapest purchase is the one you did not need.
body: Make a list before a sale starts and stick to it. Our buying guides are a starting point for items worth owning.

faq.q: What is a good discount on Amazon?
faq.a: There is no fixed percentage. A good discount is one that brings the price near or below the item's lowest recent price.
Some are, some are not. Treat them like any other sale: check the price history and seller first.

faq.q: Can I get a refund if the price drops after I buy?
faq.a: Amazon does not generally offer price matching on its own drops. Its holiday return window, through January 31, 2027 for most items bought November 1 to December 31, 2026, can give you room to return and rebuy.
